# [EP 8: The Data Room]{.flow} {.title}

## Show me the data

This morning rival chain MunchCorp bragged in a press release about their "data-driven growth." The evidence attached: exactly **one pie chart.** The investor slid it across the table: *"Yours will be better. Show me the data."*

. . .

Tobi didn't wait. He'd pasted the question into a chatbot, proudly turned the laptop around, and hit run:

`AttributeError: 'DataFrame' object has no attribute 'overview'`

. . .

The AI sounded certain. The method it called **does not exist.** Today starts with the tool that answers the investor for real, **pandas**, and then comes back to that difference.

# [The DataFrame]{.flow} {.title}

## What pandas adds over NumPy

Last session, a NumPy array turned a thousand numbers into one fast object, but every value had to share **one type**, and columns had no names.

- A **DataFrame** is a table: named columns, and each column can be a different type
- Text zones next to float euros next to integer counts, all in one object
- It's the spreadsheet the investor handed you, loaded into Python

. . .

The convention everyone uses: `import pandas as pd`.

## A DataFrame from a dictionary

Keys become **column names**; each list becomes a **column**; one order per row, mixed types together:

```{python}
#| eval: true
#| output-location: fragment

import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "order_id":  [101, 102, 103, 104, 105],
    "zone":      ["Nord", "Sued", "Nord", "Hafen", "Sued"],
    "items":     [2, 1, 3, 1, 4],
    "total_eur": [18.50, 7.20, 24.00, 6.80, 31.40],
})
print(df)
```

## A DataFrame from a file

:::{.callout-note}
Nobody types two weeks of orders by hand: today's lab loads a real **CSV** (a table saved as plain text, one row per line) in one line, `orders = pd.read_csv("orders_messy.csv")`. The file sits in the same folder as your script, so its name is all the path you need.
:::

## First look: `.head()` and `.info()`

Glance at a table first. `.head()` shows the top rows; `.info()` is your first sanity check: right number of rows? Any surprising type?

```{python}
#| eval: true
#| output-location: fragment

print(df.head(3))     # first 3 rows
df.info()             # columns, dtypes, non-null counts
```

## Numbers at a glance: `.describe()`

`.describe()` computes count, mean, min, max and quartiles for every **numeric** column at once:

```{python}
#| eval: true
#| output-location: fragment

print(df.describe())
```

. . .

One call, the whole numeric summary: this is the `.overview()` Tobi's chatbot wished existed, under its real name.

## Selecting a column

Pick one column by name:

```{python}
#| eval: true
#| output-location: fragment

print(df["zone"])                  # one column (a Series)
```

## Filtering rows

Keep rows with a **boolean mask**, exactly the NumPy idea from last session:

```{python}
#| eval: true
#| output-location: fragment

print(df[df["zone"] == "Nord"])    # only the Nord rows, case-sensitive!
```

. . .

`df["zone"] == "Nord"` builds a column of `True`/`False`; indexing with it keeps the `True` rows. `.loc` exists for label-based selection, but a plain mask covers today.

## Predict: what comes back?

Tobi wants the orders over 20 EUR. He compares the column and prints the result:

```python
big = df["total_eur"] > 20
print(big)
```

a\) a column of `True`/`False`, one per row\
b\) only the rows whose total is over 20\
c\) a single `True`, since some order is over 20


## Answer: a mask, not a table

```{python}
#| eval: true
#| output-location: fragment

big = df["total_eur"] > 20
print(big)              # the mask: a Series of booleans
print(df[big])          # the rows: build the mask, then apply it
```

. . .

**a) a column of `True`/`False`**. The comparison alone is the **mask**, a Series with one boolean per row. The rows only appear once you index with it.

## Adding a column, sorting

Compute a new column from existing ones, then sort. Work on a **copy** so the original stays intact:

```{python}
#| eval: true
#| output-location: fragment

priced = df.copy()
priced["eur_per_item"] = priced["total_eur"] / priced["items"]
print(priced.sort_values("total_eur", ascending=False))
```

. . .

`sort_values` reorders rows by a column, biggest orders first here. The new column is just arithmetic on two others, computed for every row at once.

## Predict: filter, wrong case

Tobi filters for the Nord zone, but types it **lowercase**. The data spells it `"Nord"`. What does this print?

```python
print(df[df["zone"] == "nord"])
```

a\) an empty table, no error\
b\) the Nord rows anyway: case is ignored\
c\) a `KeyError` for the missing zone


## Answer: an empty table, no warning

```{python}
#| eval: true
#| output-location: fragment

print(df[df["zone"] == "nord"])          # nothing matches "nord"
print("rows:", len(df[df["zone"] == "nord"]))
```

. . .

**a) an empty table**. `"nord"` matches nothing, so the mask is all `False` and pandas hands back **zero rows**. No error, no complaint.

. . .

This is the dangerous kind of bug: it **runs**, it just returns nothing. **pandas won't warn you; YOU verify**, which is exactly why you test filters on a case whose answer you know.

## One more tool: `groupby`

The investor's real question is **per zone**: which area brings in the most?

- `groupby` splits the table by a category, then computes **once per group**
- `df.groupby("zone")["total_eur"].sum()` → one total for each zone

. . .

:::{.callout-note}
That's the teaser: the lab needs more of `groupby` than this slide shows. It is a good one to **ask your agent** about. How to check what it hands you comes next.
:::

# [AI joins the team]{.flow} {.title}

## Prompting: context + constraints

Two things turn a vague request into a useful answer:

- **Context**. Say what the data *is*: "I have a DataFrame `orders` with columns `zone` (text) and `total_eur` (float)."
- **Constraints**. Say exactly what you want *back*: "Give me the total `total_eur` for zone `Nord`, as a single number."

. . .

> *"DataFrame `orders`, text column `zone`, float column `total_eur`. Write one line that returns the total `total_eur` where `zone` is `Nord`."*

Vague in, vague out. Specific in, checkable out, then you **iterate**.

## The verify workflow

Tobi's mistake wasn't *using* AI. It was **shipping without checking.** Every line an AI hands you gets three passes:

1. **Read it**: do you understand what each line claims to do?
2. **Run it**: does it actually execute, or does it crash?
3. **Test it**: try it on a small case where **you already know the answer.**

## Step 3 in action

Five orders with values you can add in your head, and the AI's suggested line for the Nord average:

```{python}
#| eval: true
#| output-location: fragment

import pandas as pd

check = pd.DataFrame({
    "zone":      ["Nord", "Sued", "Nord", "Hafen", "Nord"],
    "total_eur": [10.0, 7.5, 20.0, 5.0, 30.0],
})
print(check[check["zone"] == "Nord"]["total_eur"].mean())
```

. . .

The Nord orders are 10, 20 and 30. You can average those in your head. Does the AI's answer match? Then the line has earned some trust on the real file. Verification is the job now, not typing.

## Predict: it ran, so it's right?

Tobi asks the AI for the **Nord average** on the same five orders. It hands back one line and calls it done. What does this print?

```python
print(check["total_eur"].mean())
```

a\) `20.0`\
b\) an `AttributeError`\
c\) `14.5`


## Answer: it ran, and it's wrong

```{python}
#| eval: true
#| output-location: fragment

print(check["total_eur"].mean())                             # every zone
print(check[check["zone"] == "Nord"]["total_eur"].mean())    # Nord only
```

. . .

**c) `14.5`**: the line averages **all five** orders. Nobody filtered for Nord, and pandas has no way to know that was the question.

. . .

No traceback, a plausible number, and still wrong. "It runs" only clears step 2; step 3 is where the investor's number gets tested.

## Predict: does `.summarize()` exist?

The AI wrote this for Tobi. `orders` is a tiny two-row frame. What happens on the last line?

```python
import pandas as pd
orders = pd.DataFrame({"zone": ["Nord", "Sued"], "total_eur": [12.0, 9.5]})

orders.summarize()
```

a\) prints a summary table\
b\) raises an `AttributeError`\
c\) returns an empty DataFrame


## Answer: the method never existed

```{python}
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| output: false
%xmode Minimal
```

```{python}
#| eval: true
#| error: true
#| output-location: fragment

import pandas as pd
orders = pd.DataFrame({"zone": ["Nord", "Sued"], "total_eur": [12.0, 9.5]})
orders.summarize()                     # the method the AI invented
```

. . .

**b) `AttributeError`**: pandas has no `.summarize()`. The AI invented it.

## The real method is `.describe()`

```{python}
#| eval: true
#| output-location: fragment

print(orders.describe())               # the method that actually exists
```

. . .

**An AI that sounds sure is not the same as an API that exists.**

## Why did it invent a method?

Session VI gave you the machine, so here is why it fails in exactly this way.

- Training rewards a [plausible]{.highlight} continuation and never checks a [true]{.highlight} one: nothing in the loop verifies facts
- And it always writes *some* next token, confident or not: a choice gets picked, printed, and it all looks equally smooth
- `.summarize` is a *plausible* pandas name: short, lowercase, shaped like `.describe()`. Plausible is what the machine optimizes for

. . .

**Fluent and wrong is not a bug to patch. It is how the machine works.**

## How it was trained, in one slide

- **Pre-training**: predict the next token over massive text, where the [weights]{.highlight} inside get adjusted; applying them afterwards is cheap
- **Fine-tuning**: curated examples teach it to follow instructions
- **RLHF** (reinforcement learning from human feedback): humans rank answers; it learns to prefer the ranked-higher ones
- Its knowledge has an end date, the [knowledge cutoff]{.highlight}: after it, it guesses fluently instead. And it inherits the [biases]{.highlight} of the text it read

. . .

Every stage rewards *sounding* right; none of them checks pandas. That is your job, and step 3 of the verify workflow is how.

## Disclosure: say what the AI did

In your project (Part III) you list each AI use in one line. Labs and checkpoints need no note, but the habit is worth starting today:

- *"Used the chatbot to draft the `groupby` line; I checked the totals by hand."*
- Standard practice, not an admission of anything.

. . .

It protects **you**: it separates the work you understand from the work you pasted, so when a reviewer (or the investor) asks "how does this line work?", you're never caught claiming something you can't explain.

## When NOT to reach for AI

Sometimes the fastest path is the one you already own. You built a whole muscle in Part I:

- A red traceback? **You've read those since Episode 5.** The last line names the error and points at the file, often faster than describing it to a chatbot.
- A one-line filter you've written ten times? Just write it.

. . .

:::{.callout-tip}
Use AI to draft the unfamiliar and to explain the confusing, not to skip thinking you can do yourself.
:::

# [Wrap-up]{.flow} {.title}

## Three things to remember

1. **A DataFrame is a named, mixed-type table.** `pd.DataFrame` from a dict, `pd.read_csv` from a file; `.head()`, `.info()`, `.describe()` to look before you leap.
2. **Select, filter, add, group.** `df["col"]`, a boolean mask (`df[df["zone"] == "Nord"]`, case-sensitive!), a new column on a `.copy()`, `groupby` per category. pandas won't warn; you verify.
3. **AI drafts, you verify.** Give it context and constraints, then read it → run it → test it on a case you know.

. . .
